summary: Discusses problems with using up the top level domain space and possible conflicts when several organizations want the same name. It aims to start discussion of how domain names might be fairly allocated. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2352.

plainLanguage.summary: It talks about what to do when many people want the same web address, and what rules might decide who gets it.

questions: how are domain names legally allocated
how should domain names be fairly allocated
how could legal registration decide domain ownership
what was the problem with the flat domain space
subtitle: A proposal to allocate domain names fairly using legal company registration.

tldr.problem: In the mid-1990s, the Internet faced a crisis: the generic top-level domains (.com, .org, etc.) were rapidly filling up, and many organizations wanted the same names, leading to disputes and conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes adding structure beneath country domains using existing legal company classifications (e.g., LTD.UK for limited companies in the UK, INC.US for US corporations). Legal registries, not DNS administrators, would decide who gets a name based on actual business registration.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was not adopted as described. RFC 2352 followed with different recommendations, and the domain space eventually expanded through new generic TLDs instead of this legal-structure approach.

today: RFC 2240 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 2352 in May 1998. The hierarchical, legally-structured domain allocation system it proposed was not adopted. Instead, the domain system expanded through new generic TLDs. However, questions of fairness and legal basis for domain allocation remain active in domain policy discussions.

sections.title: The Problem: Domain Name Exhaustion and Conflict
sections.content:
By 1997, the domain name system faced a serious problem. The generic top-level domains (gTLDs)—.com, .org, .net, and others—were organized as a flat hierarchy. Anyone could register EXAMPLE.COM, but only one person could have it. Thousands of organizations wanted the same names (FORD could be a car company, a law firm, or a river), and the system had no way to resolve these conflicts fairly.

At the same time, the entire top-level domain space was in danger of exhaustion. The proposal being debated at the time was to add new gTLDs like .FIRM, .STORE, and .WEB, allowing the same name to exist under multiple TLDs. But this created new problems: would MCDONALDS.COM refer to the restaurant or a law firm? Large companies would simply reserve all variations of their name, making exhaustion worse.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone wanted the same web addresses, but only one person could have each one. Creating more web address endings like .FIRM and .STORE didn't help, because then big companies would grab all versions of their name.

sections.title: The Hierarchical Solution: Legal Domain Categories
sections.content:
Rather than flattening the domain space further, this RFC proposes using the existing hierarchical structure of country domains. Instead of just EXAMPLE.FR for France, the system would create second-level domains like LTD.FR (for French limited companies), SARL.FR (for Sociétés à Responsabilité Limitée), and others based on each country's actual legal business classifications.

An organization wanting a domain name would first prove its legal right to a name (by showing business registration), then claim that name under the appropriate legal category. FORD.LTD.UK would belong to the Ford Motor Company as a UK-registered company; a French law firm could have FORD.SARL.FR. The decision of who gets a name would move from DNS administrators to the legitimate company registration authorities in each country.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of everyone competing for FORD.COM, the system would let the real Ford Motor Company have FORD.LTD.UK (using their legal company type), and a French firm could use FORD.SARL.FR (using France's legal company type). A government registry, not the Internet, would decide if you really owned the company.

sections.title: Proposed Structure and Allocation
sections.content:
Each country would create second-level domains (SLDs) matching its legal business types. In the UK, this might be LTD.UK (limited companies) and PLC.UK (public companies). In the US, INC.US (incorporated bodies) and CORP.US (corporations). Germany would use GMBH.DE. For international entities and trademarks, the INT domain would provide TM.INT and REG.INT.

The registries managing country domains would enforce the legal basis for allocation. When a company applied for a domain name, it would provide evidence of legal registration. The registry would validate the application using the actual laws of the country. This made disputes nearly impossible: if you were a registered Limited Company in the UK, no other UK Limited Company could have your exact name.

The system would still allow less-formal registrations for organizations that did not fit legal categories (NGOs, government bodies, academic institutions), possibly under generic SLDs like ORG.UK or AC.UK, but the legal categories would provide a clear, unambiguous hierarchy for registered companies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each country would organize domains by business type: LTD.UK for limited companies, GMBH.DE for German companies, INC.US for US corporations. A business would register under its legal type, proved by a business license or registration certificate.

sections.title: Advantages and Implementation Challenges
sections.content:
The proposal had clear advantages. Disputes would disappear: all names under LTD.UK would be unique because no two UK limited companies can have identical registered names. The burden of determining who deserves a name would shift from DNS administrators (who lack legal authority) to company registration authorities (who are mandated by law to prevent duplicate registrations). Name exhaustion would become impossible—anyone with a legal company registration would automatically have a right to a matching domain name.

However, the proposal faced practical challenges. Different countries have different legal structures, making standardization difficult. Non-ASCII identifiers in languages using non-Roman alphabets were not yet supported by DNS and domain name systems. Organizations would need to understand a more complex naming structure. Some argued the system was overly complicated for what the Internet community wanted.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea solved the conflict problem completely, but it meant learning a lot of different rules for different countries, and computers weren't ready to handle names in non-English languages yet.

sections.title: Outcome and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 2240 was published as Informational in November 1997, meaning it did not set a standard; rather, it was a proposal for discussion. The community's response led to RFC 2352, which offered a somewhat different approach. Ultimately, the domain name system evolved differently: new generic TLDs were added (including gTLDs like .BIZ, .INFO, and later hundreds more), and the hierarchical, legally-structured approach proposed here was not adopted.

However, the RFC remains relevant to discussions about domain name policy, intellectual property protection in the domain system, and the tension between fair allocation and practical simplicity. Some modern initiatives, such as country-code TLD policies, do incorporate elements of legal verification, though not at the scale and structure proposed in RFC 2240.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet didn't adopt this plan. Instead, they added more endings like .BIZ and .INFO. But the idea of using legal proof to decide who gets a domain name still comes up in policy discussions today.
